headline: Colom's lead grows; Ukraine prisoner swap agreed; Carney heads abroad
briefing: Democrat Scott Colom's lead in Mississippi's uncalled U.S. Senate race grew to 4,404 votes on Wednesday, and the White House warned Democrats that their planned investigations could be treated as crimes. Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large prisoner swap but nothing on ending the war, and oil climbed back above US$93. At home, Prime Minister Carney left for summits in Dublin and Asia, and criticism of Ontario's appointed regional chairs spread from York to Muskoka.

keyDates.label: Dublin summit; Witkoff in Moscow
keyDates.why: Carney joins about 50 leaders at the European Political Community summit on Ukraine while U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff meets Putin.

keyDates.label: Mississippi county results due
keyDates.why: Counties must send certified results in the close Colom–Hyde-Smith Senate race to the secretary of state by Friday.

keyDates.label: New municipal term begins
keyDates.why: Ontario councils elected Oct. 26 and the newly appointed regional chairs begin their four-year term.

keyDates.label: APEC summit; Alaska ranked-choice count
keyDates.why: Carney meets Xi in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, and Alaska tabulates its Peltola–Sullivan Senate race.

keyDates.label: Bill 140 comments close
keyDates.why: Last day for public comments on the province's environmental-law changes on the Environmental Registry.

keyDates.label: Bank of Canada and Fed rate decisions
keyDates.why: Both central banks decide the same day; hot U.S. inflation and oil prices keep further hikes on the table.

stories.headline: Colom's Mississippi lead grows to 4,404 after Hinds County finishes count
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom widened his lead over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday after Mississippi's largest Democratic county finished its provisional ballots; the race is still uncalled.
stories.now: The Associated Press count on Wednesday put Scott Colom 4,404 votes ahead of Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith with about 99% of the vote counted, up from roughly 3,000 earlier in the day. Hinds County election commissioners accepted 817 of 2,426 affidavit (provisional) ballots and rejected 1,609; Colom won 703 of the accepted ones to Hyde-Smith's 96. Counties must send official results to the secretary of state by Friday, Mississippi has no automatic recount law, and Senate Republicans' campaign arm has asked counties to set aside and preserve affidavit ballots, a sign a legal challenge is possible. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in first-choice votes in the last update, and the ranked-choice count runs on Nov. 18. Democrats are projected to hold at least 259 House seats and a Senate majority either way.
stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.

timeline.event: Supreme Court rejects bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
Cooper projected to flip North Carolina; Ossoff holds Georgia
Democrats win both chambers; Vance blames Iran war
Hinds County finishes; Colom lead reaches 4,404

stories.why: Democratic control of both chambers means the administration will face subpoenas, investigations and legislative roadblocks starting in January, and trade and tariff policy could be contested in Congress.
stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.

stories.headline: Russia and Ukraine agree to large prisoner swap; U.S. envoy heads to Moscow
stories.summary: Two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi ended Wednesday with agreement on a large prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war; envoy Steve Witkoff sees Putin on Thursday, then Zelenskyy in Dublin.
stories.now: Ukraine's lead negotiator Rustem Umerov said the main result of the Abu Dhabi round was agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange, and Russia's Vladimir Medinsky confirmed a deal in principle with details to follow. U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said the numbers would be finalized Thursday; before the talks Zelenskyy had described formats of 1,000 or 1,500 prisoners per side. Medinsky said the sides found common ground on some issues but not others, and there was no visible movement on territory or a ceasefire. Witkoff is due in Moscow on Thursday to meet President Vladimir Putin, then flies to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy, where about 50 leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, gather Thursday for the European Political Community summit focused on Ukraine and European security.
stories.backstory: U.S.-mediated efforts to end the war stalled for months while Washington focused on Iran. Rubio said in May that the effort had stagnated. Europe has repeatedly asked to be included in any deal affecting its own security.

timeline.event: Rubio says peace effort has stagnated
Large prisoner swap agreed in principle
Witkoff due in Moscow, then Dublin

stories.why: A deal, or a breakdown, would shape European security and Canada's allied commitments. Disagreement between the U.S. and Europe is also a risk.
stories.impact: Peace progress could ease energy and grain prices over time. Canada, a NATO and G7 member, would feel the effects of any change in security arrangements.

stories.headline: Oil climbs back above US$93 as Iran talks stall and blockade stays
stories.summary: Brent crude rose more than 2% on Wednesday to about US$93 a barrel as shipping attacks near the Strait of Hormuz and stalled diplomacy offset hopes for a Qatar-brokered deal.
stories.now: Brent traded between roughly US$92 and US$94 on Wednesday and was last quoted a little above US$93, up more than 2% from Tuesday, when it dipped below US$90 for the first time since August; U.S. benchmark WTI (West Texas Intermediate) was near US$87. Trump said this week he will hold off on new strikes but keep the naval blockade, and a new U.S. task force is meant to choke overland and Caspian Sea trade into Iran. Iran's reported offer would reopen the strait in exchange for an end to the blockade and some sanctions relief; Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Tehran's latest terms outrageous, and senior Iranian figure Mohsen Rezaei dismissed the talks as imaginary. Trump said Wednesday the U.S. had won the war, a claim Iran rejected. Separately, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was reported to have moved to a military base over Iranian threats.
stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.

timeline.event: June deal collapses; U.S. blockade begins
Qatar hands Iran a new draft deal
Qatar PM meets Trump; Brent falls ~7%
Brent dips below US$90, rebounds above US$93

stories.why: Oil prices are the main driver of higher inflation in Canada and the U.S.; the October spike is why the Bank of Canada raised rates on Oct. 28.
stories.impact: Lower crude usually reaches GTA gas pumps within days, which would ease fuel and delivery costs. A failed deal or new attacks on shipping could quickly reverse the drop.

stories.headline: Ousted Muskoka chair 'deeply disappointed' as backlash to Ford's regional picks grows
stories.summary: A day after Ontario named eight regional heads with 'strong chair' powers, Muskoka's replaced chair Jeff Lehman voiced his disappointment and Markham's mayor kept up criticism of Steven Del Duca's York appointment.
stories.now: Jeff Lehman, who was Muskoka's district chair until the province replaced him with Scott Aitchison, said Wednesday he was deeply disappointed by the decision. In York, Markham Mayor Frank Scarpitti called new chair Steven Del Duca, who stays on as Vaughan's mayor, deeply conflicted and no friend of Markham, and said the job gives one person overriding power over nine mayors and a roughly $5.2-billion regional budget. Del Duca said he will speak for all nine York municipalities and that none can be left behind. Municipal Affairs Minister Rob Flack rejected claims the picks are party insiders, noting Del Duca once led the Ontario Liberals; the other appointees are Kevin Ashe (Durham), Ann Mulvale (Halton), Frank Campion (Niagara), Nando Iannicca (Peel), Scott Davey (Waterloo) and Don McIsaac as Simcoe County warden. The chairs can hire or fire senior staff, veto some bylaws and propose the regional budget, and their term starts Nov. 15.
stories.backstory: Ontario first gave 'strong mayor' powers to Toronto and Ottawa in 2022 and later extended them to dozens of cities. This spring the province brought in the Better Regional Governance Act, letting it appoint chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka, Peel, Waterloo and York and the Simcoe warden, and cutting the size of Niagara's council. Some of these posts were previously chosen by voters or by regional councillors. The appointments come right after the Oct. 26 municipal elections.

timeline.event: Strong mayor powers for Toronto and Ottawa
Ousted Muskoka chair and Markham mayor object

stories.why: Regional governments run water, sewers, police budgets, roads and much of the planning that decides where housing goes. Appointed chairs with veto and staffing powers shift control toward Queen's Park.
stories.impact: For York, Peel, Durham and Halton residents, regional chairs now have more say over budgets that drive property taxes and over approvals for housing and infrastructure. Watch the first regional budgets under the new chairs.

stories.headline: White House warns Democrats their planned probes could be 'criminality'
stories.summary: The White House's top lawyer told the incoming Democratic chair of the House Oversight Committee that promised investigations of the Trump administration could cross into criminal conduct; Democrats say they will not back down.
stories.now: White House counsel Will Scharf wrote to Rep. Robert Garcia, who is set to chair the House Oversight Committee in January, arguing that threats meant to deter officials from serving, or legal demands meant to intimidate them, could amount to crimes. Garcia replied that it looks as though Trump has something to hide and that Congress's power to investigate does not depend on White House approval. Incoming Judiciary chair Jamie Raskin called the warning meaningless, and Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called it outrageous. Democrats have signalled probes of White House construction projects including the ballroom, the Trump family's role in mineral deals and its cryptocurrency dealings. Reports differ on whether the letter was dated Monday or sent Wednesday.
stories.backstory: Democrats won both chambers of Congress on Nov. 3 and take control in January, which gives their committee chairs subpoena power for the first time in Trump's second term. Garcia said before the election that officials could face subpoenas on day one. Oversight of the executive branch is a routine function of Congress, though administrations of both parties have resisted it.

timeline.event: White House letter to Garcia made public

stories.why: It signals that the White House plans to fight congressional investigations hard, which points to subpoena battles and court fights for much of 2027.
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on Ontario, but a Washington consumed by investigations may have less room for trade deals, and probes could touch tariff and minerals decisions that matter to Canadian exporters.

sources.title: MPR News/AP: White House confronts Democrats over planned probes

stories.headline: Carney leaves for Dublin summit, then Asia and a meeting with Xi
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney flew out after the Remembrance Day ceremony for an eight-day trip to Ireland, the Philippines, Cambodia and China, ending at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.
stories.now: Carney left Ottawa on Wednesday after laying a wreath at the National War Memorial and was due in Dublin by late afternoon local time. On Thursday he attends the European Political Community summit, where about 50 leaders will focus on Ukraine and European security; Canada is again the only non-European country at the table. He is scheduled to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Saturday, then visits Cambodia before the APEC leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19. There he plans to tell Chinese President Xi Jinping that Canada will not accept foreign interference, while pursuing what he calls a deeper economic partnership with guardrails.
stories.backstory: A federal public inquiry found that China was the most active foreign state trying to interfere in Canada's democratic institutions. Relations soured for years over arrests, tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and Chinese duties on Canadian canola. Carney's government has since sought to rebuild trade ties with Beijing as tariffs from the Trump administration hit Canadian exports, which drew a tariff threat from Trump over any Canada-China deal.

timeline.event: Carney calls China Canada's top geopolitical threat
Carney visits China; new partnership announced
Carney says he will raise interference with Xi

stories.why: The trip is part of Ottawa's effort to rely less on the United States for trade and defence. How Carney balances business with Beijing against security worries and pressure from Washington affects farmers, automakers and diaspora communities.
stories.impact: GTA residents with family or business ties to China are among those most exposed to interference concerns. Any trade easing could matter for Ontario exporters and for car buyers, while friction with the U.S. over China ties could complicate Canada-U.S. trade talks.

stories.headline: Absent Democrats let Hegseth impeachment die; House GOP picks Jim Jordan as leader
stories.summary: Eleven Democrats missed Tuesday's 211-204 vote that shelved impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, enough to have changed the result, and House Republicans chose Jim Jordan to lead them in the minority.
stories.now: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to send Rep. Thomas Massie's eight impeachment articles to the Judiciary Committee, ending the effort for this Congress. Eleven Democrats were absent; had all voted no, the motion would have failed 215-211. Several, including Reps. Melanie Stansbury, Marilyn Strickland and Jonathan Jackson, blamed traffic and a police escort near the Capitol, while Nancy Pelosi had flown to San Francisco for a Veterans Day event and others cited medical or personal reasons; colleagues criticized the absences on Wednesday. Trump said the effort had failed miserably. Also Tuesday, House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as their leader for the next Congress, 106-73 over Majority Leader Steve Scalise, after Speaker Mike Johnson declined to seek the post.
stories.backstory: Massie's articles centre on the Iran war, which he says has run more than 90 days without approval from Congress, and also cite operations in Venezuela and Yemen. He first filed them in the fall, but the House left early for the campaign. Democrats won the House in the Nov. 3 midterms and take control in January; their leader Hakeem Jeffries calls himself a hard yes on impeachment.

timeline.event: Jeffries says he is a hard yes
House shelves them 211-204; GOP elects Jordan

stories.why: The impeachment push is over for now, but Democrats can revive it or hold hearings on the Iran war once they control the House in January. Jordan's win suggests House Republicans will take a combative line against the new majority.
stories.impact: The effects for Ontario are indirect: fights over the Iran war and Pentagon policy can shape oil prices and U.S. defence and trade priorities. Watch for how a divided Washington handles tariffs and Canada talks.

stories.headline: Bank of Canada notes show oil shock drove its October rate hike
stories.summary: The central bank's summary of its Oct. 28 deliberations says officials weighed holding at 2.25% against hiking to 2.5%, and chose the hike mainly because oil prices looked set to stay high for longer.
stories.now: The Bank of Canada published its summary of Governing Council talks on Tuesday afternoon. Members considered two options, holding the policy rate at 2.25% or raising it to 2.5%, and the main reason they hiked was that oil prices tied to the Middle East war were expected to stay elevated. They also judged that stronger growth would use up spare capacity in the economy and that rising business costs would eventually show up in core inflation. Since the decision, Brent crude has fallen roughly 20% from its late-October peak, which could ease that worry. The next rate decision is Dec. 9.
stories.backstory: The bank cut its key rate to 2.25% in October 2025 as tariffs slowed the economy. Energy prices then surged with the Iran war, and annual inflation reached 3.1% in September, although core measures stayed near 2%. On Oct. 28 the bank raised its rate a quarter point to 2.5%, its first hike in about three years, and said further increases might be needed.
stories.why: The bank's rate sets the prime rate that variable mortgages and lines of credit follow. Its reasoning shows that falling oil prices could reduce the case for another hike.
stories.impact: GTA homeowners with variable-rate mortgages or renewing soon should watch Dec. 9. If oil keeps falling, pressure for another increase may ease; if it rebounds, borrowing costs could rise again.

stories.headline: Ottawa widens tariff relief as Carney says Trump still calls the shots on trade
stories.summary: Ottawa widened its tariff relief program to more imported goods, and Carney said the Trump administration remains the key player on a trade deal despite Democratic midterm wins.
stories.now: The federal government extended its tariff relief program beyond U.S. steel imports, so goods used by public education bodies, including those mandated by Indigenous organizations, can also qualify; Newsweek reports the program now runs to June 30, 2028, while exemptions are being withdrawn for some U.S. goods where Canadian alternatives exist. On Tuesday, Carney said the Trump administration remains the main authority on trade agreements even after Democrats won Congress, and Ottawa will keep working toward a deal that suits Canada. Democrats have pledged to try to repeal tariffs on Canada, but they would need Republican votes to override a veto. Trump has also threatened new tariffs on Canadian vehicles starting in January.
stories.backstory: Canada has used remission and relief measures to soften the cost of counter-tariffs on its own importers. A recent Finance Canada report found Ottawa approved about $5.6 billion in relief against a projected $2.2 billion, with more than 800 requests still unresolved.

stories.why: Counter-tariffs raise costs for Canadian buyers, so relief rules decide who pays more.
stories.impact: Schools and some public bodies in Ontario may face lower costs on imported goods. Businesses importing affected goods may be able to apply for relief.

stories.headline: U.S. prices rise 0.4% in October as energy costs bite
stories.summary: The U.S. consumer price index rose 0.4% in October, above forecasts, keeping pressure on the Federal Reserve ahead of its December decision.
stories.now: The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said consumer prices rose 0.4% in October after a 0.6% jump in September, beating the 0.3% economists expected. Energy rose 0.7%, food 0.5% and shelter 0.3%, while core prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3% for a third straight month. The BLS did not publish a year-over-year rate because last year's government shutdown stopped October 2025 data collection; one economist puts the implied annual pace around 4%. Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi said the report makes a December rate increase more likely.
stories.backstory: Oil prices surged after the U.S.-Iran war began in February and the Strait of Hormuz was choked, pushing up fuel and shipping costs. U.S. inflation has run well above the Fed's 2% target for months, and tariffs have added to the price of many imported goods. The Fed and the Bank of Canada both announce rate decisions on Dec. 9.
stories.why: Hotter U.S. inflation makes another Fed hike more likely, which tends to push up borrowing costs and the U.S. dollar.
stories.impact: A stronger U.S. dollar makes cross-border shopping and U.S. travel pricier for GTA residents. Rate moves in the U.S. also influence Canadian fixed mortgage rates and the Bank of Canada's December thinking.

stories.headline: Experts warn Ford's Bill 140 would gut Ontario's Environmental Bill of Rights
stories.summary: Environmental lawyers and advocacy groups say the Ford government's Building Ontario Faster Act would strip key public rights to comment on and challenge environmental decisions; public comments close Nov. 26.
stories.now: Bill 140, the Building Ontario Faster Act, 2026, was tabled on Oct. 27 and would amend 23 laws and create two new ones. Critics focus on Schedule 8, which rewrites the Environmental Bill of Rights (EBR); Richard Lindgren of the Canadian Environmental Law Association (CELA) says the law would keep its name but lose the legal rights people actually use. Groups including Environmental Defence say it would weaken public consultation, remove appeal rights and drop some notices from the Environmental Registry of Ontario. The bill also changes the Environmental Assessment Act and the Environmental Protection Act. The province has said the changes are meant to speed up housing and infrastructure.
stories.backstory: Ontario's EBR, passed in 1993, lets residents comment on proposed environmental decisions and, in some cases, seek leave to appeal permits. The Ford government has repeatedly moved to fast-track projects, including 2025's Bill 5, which weakened species-at-risk protections and allowed special economic zones. It also exempted the proposed Dresden landfill from a full environmental assessment, a move local councils still oppose.

timeline.event: Dresden landfill exempted from full assessment
Legal experts warn of lost public rights

stories.why: The bill would decide how much say residents have over landfills, quarries, highways and industrial permits near their homes. Supporters say faster approvals help build housing; critics say they shut the public out.
stories.impact: GTA residents near proposed developments, aggregate pits or waste sites may have fewer ways to object or appeal. You can still comment on the Environmental Registry of Ontario until Nov. 26.

stories.headline: Treasury's Bessent moved to a military base after Iranian threats
stories.summary: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has left his Washington home for a military base because of threats linked to Iran, according to multiple news reports citing unnamed officials.
stories.now: The New York Times first reported the move, and Reuters, the Associated Press and others have since matched it through unnamed sources; officials have not said when it happened. A senior administration official told Fox News the threats had gone beyond an advanced stage. Bessent has led the sanctions campaign against Iran's economy, and a Treasury spokesperson said he will not be deterred. Reuters reported that concern grew after a newspaper published an aerial photo of his Georgetown house. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller are also reported to be living in protected military housing.
stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Washington has since added a naval blockade and tighter sanctions. Western officials have warned of Iran-linked plots abroad; on Tuesday, U.S. prosecutors charged three men with directing attacks in Europe and the U.S. and planning an assault on RAF Fairford, a British base used by American bombers.

timeline.event: Bessent steps up economic pressure on Iran
U.S. charges three in alleged Iran-backed plots
Reports say Bessent moved to a base

stories.why: It shows the Iran war reaching senior U.S. officials at home, and it adds to the pressure around any deal to end the conflict.
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on Ontario and no known Canadian link. It is a reminder that security alerts tied to the war could persist even if oil prices ease.

stories.headline: Spain holds first general strike in 14 years over housing costs
stories.summary: Unions say about four million workers walked out on Wednesday to demand action on housing and wages, less than three weeks before a snap national election.
stories.now: Spain's two largest union federations, UGT and CCOO, led the 24-hour stoppage and put participation at about four million workers; employers dispute the unions' figures. CCOO leader Unai Sordo said turnout beat expectations. Support was strongest in the public sector, industry and coastal regions where housing pressure is most severe, and weaker in hospitality and finance. Police reported at least 27 arrests, with a later count of 29, nine of them in Madrid. The unions want more government intervention in the housing market, full use of the national housing law in every region and a new minimum-wage agreement.
stories.backstory: Rents and home prices in Spain have climbed much faster than wages, and big housing marches filled Madrid and other cities in early October. The eviction of an 87-year-old Madrid woman became a rallying point. Spain votes in a snap general election on Nov. 29, and polls suggest the far right could enter government. The last general strike was in 2012.

timeline.event: Mass housing protests in Madrid and other cities
General strike; unions claim four million

stories.why: Housing costs are now driving national politics in a major European economy, and the strike could shape an election in which the far right may gain power.
stories.impact: There is no direct effect here, but the dispute mirrors the GTA's own affordability squeeze. Anyone travelling to Spain should expect normal service to resume Thursday.

stories.headline: Canadians mark Remembrance Day as Carney and Arbour lay wreaths in Ottawa
stories.summary: Ceremonies across the country and the GTA honoured Canada's veterans and war dead, with the national service in Ottawa and events at Old City Hall and Queen's Park in Toronto.
stories.now: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Governor General Louise Arbour laid wreaths at the National War Memorial in Ottawa during the Royal Canadian Legion's national ceremony, which included a CF-18 flypast and a 21-gun salute. Carney described remembrance as an act of vigilance and determination and again mourned the four soldiers killed in last month's fire at CFB Wainwright. In Toronto, ceremonies were held at 10:45 a.m. at the Old City Hall Cenotaph and Queen's Park, with nearby road closures, and the TTC paused service for two minutes at 11 a.m. This year also marks 25 years since Canada's mission in Afghanistan began.
stories.backstory: Remembrance Day marks the 1918 armistice that ended the First World War and honours Canadians who served and died in conflicts since. It is not a statutory holiday in Ontario, so most businesses and schools stay open, while federal workers get the day off. This year's ceremonies follow the Oct. 17 fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta that killed four soldiers and injured 39; three investigations are under way.

timeline.event: Fire at CFB Wainwright kills four soldiers

stories.why: It is the country's main day to honour military service, and this year comes weeks after a deadly training accident.
stories.impact: Downtown Toronto road closures near Queen and Bay and Queen's Park have been lifted. Most Ontario stores and services stayed open; federal offices and Canada Post were closed for the day.
